# Thinking — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/thinking.html

Thinking — Varun Velhankar

Thinking

Design is a decision-making discipline. My job is to make the right decisions visible, and the wrong ones impossible to ship.

Two halves of the same practice: how I design AI agents people can trust, and how I lead design and build teams so the right calls get made fast.

Part one · Designing agents

Designing AI-native products users can trust.

01Autonomy is a dial, not a switch

Every action an agent can take gets its own setting: decide, ask, or hand off. Two questions set it. How much does a mistake cost? Can it be undone? Not: what can the model technically do?

Booking a tourDecides
Changing a move-in dateAsks
Lease exceptionHands off

02Design the handoff before the happy path

Trust is won or lost the moment an agent says “this isn’t mine to decide.” I design that moment first: what the renter is told, what the person on the other end receives in Vida, and how fast the loop closes.

03If it can’t be undone, explain it first

Reversible steps move fast. Irreversible ones slow down, show their reasoning and wait for a yes. Signatures, payments and anything legal never happen silently.

04Operators need a cockpit, not a chat log

Nobody supervises a portfolio by reading transcripts. Vida leads with what needs a human now, why, and the one action that fixes it.

05Every AI state is a design state

Thinking, confident, uncertain, escalated, completed. Each one looks and reads the same everywhere, so renters and operators always know where things stand.

ThinkingConfidentUncertainEscalatedCompleted

Part two · Leading design

Process scales teams. Judgment scales impact.

I keep the artefacts that sharpen thinking and drop the ones that only look productive. The aim is confident decisions and fast learning loops.

The loop

Align. Success metrics, owners, timeline01

Discover. Research until the problem is sharp02

Define. Strategy, architecture, constraints03

Design. Iterate and validate with users04

Deliver. Handoff, build support, UX QA05

Evolve. Measure, learn, feed the roadmap06

How I partner

With product. PMs co-own the experience. I help shape the roadmap by user impact, and push back on scope with data, not ego.

With engineering. Engineers are design partners. I bring them in at discovery and check feasibility before committing to a pattern.

Handoff is a ceremony. Annotated specs with states, edge cases and accessibility notes, a live walkthrough, and me on hand through the build.

QA is design’s job too. Nothing ships without UX QA against the spec and WCAG 2.1 AA. I sign off builds with the rigour of a code review.

A design roadmap. Research sprints, system work and UX debt get their own milestones, so leadership sees design capacity before the crunch.

Guardrails built in. Compliance, privacy and accessibility are designed in from the start, not bolted on at legal review.

Always

Users first, always.

Data informs. Intuition leads.

Design is a team sport.

Constraints breed creativity.

Ship with intention. Iterate with purpose.

Accessibility is not optional.

Part three · How I build teams

Teams scale judgment. Rituals don’t.

I’ve led a team of 5 designers at Fairstone Bank, owning hiring, budgeting, scoping and the design backlog, and a multi-country team at WebBeds across Spain, the UK, Romania and Dubai, where we took UX maturity from stage 0 to stage 3. Now I’m building Property Vista’s design function from the ground up. The same principles hold at every size:

Hire for judgment and range. I look for designers who can make a good call with half the information, and who can move between research, systems and pixels. A paid work sample beats a whiteboard puzzle.

Small, senior, close to the work. Player-coaches over layers. I set direction, review the work in detail, and still design, so the bar is visible rather than described.

Clear decision rights. Everyone knows which calls are theirs, which need a review, and which come to me. Fewer meetings, faster and better decisions.

Critique as evidence. Crits run on data, user sessions and principles, not opinion or seniority. Disagreements end in an experiment, not a vote.

Grow people on two paths. Separate IC and manager tracks, written expectations for each level, and a growth conversation every quarter, not just at review time.

Design beyond the design team. At Fairstone I trained 8+ BAs, BSAs and product owners in Figma and design thinking, so good decisions happened without a designer in every room.

The measure is simple: the team makes good calls when I’m not in the room.

TL;DR

I don’t just design screens. I design the conditions for good decisions, for the people on the team and for the agents we ship.

Designing agents of your own, or need design leadership for a season? See how I work with teams.

Say hello at varunuxd@gmail.com or on LinkedIn, or read my résumé.

# About — Varun Velhankar

About — Varun Velhankar

About

I bring structure to messy, high-stakes problems, then I ship the answer. I’m Head of Design at Property Vista, building Vivian, an AI agent that talks to renters and residents, and Vida, the console property teams use to run her.

Before this: 12+ years designing regulated banking, global travel and government platforms. I lead teams, and I still make the work.

Based in Guelph, ON (Greater Toronto Area) · remote or hybrid · Résumé · PDF ↓

How I work

Structure in ambiguity. I turn vague, high-stakes problems into a plan a team can act on this week.

Stories that land. I make complex ideas easy to follow, whether the room is executives, engineers or customers.

Range before commitment. I explore many options fast, so the one we ship has beaten real alternatives.

Close to the code. I work in the trenches with engineers, from QA reviews to fixing small bugs in production.

# Work with me — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work-with-me.html

Work with me — Varun Velhankar

Work with me

Fractional design leadership and advisory for teams building AI products where the agent does the work and people stay in control.

I’m Head of Design at Property Vista, where I designed Vivian and Vida: time-to-lease down 60%, 92% of inquiries handled without staff, and 4.4x higher lead-to-appointment conversion across properties running Vida. I take on a small number of outside engagements, in Canada and the US, remote or hybrid.

Who it’s for

Founders and product leaders. shipping an AI agent or copilot and unsure how much it should decide on its own

Seed to Series C B2B SaaS. with no design leader yet, or one who needs a senior partner

PropTech, fintech and regulated products. where trust, compliance and handoffs to people are the product

Ways to work together

Fractional Head of Design2–3 days a week
For seed to Series C teams that need senior design leadership before, or while, they hire full-time. I own design direction, set up the system and rituals, ship work myself, and help you hire my successor.

AI product design sprint2–4 weeks
For one hard AI problem: an agent’s autonomy model, a human-in-the-loop handoff, an operator console. You get a tested prototype, the decision policy behind it, and a spec your engineers can build.

AI-native design practice4–6 weeks
Set up the stack and the habits: Claude, Claude Code, Codex and Figma for concept-to-prototype in days, a design system with AI states, and synthetic plus solo user testing.

AdvisoryMonthly
A standing session with your product and design leads: reviews of agent experiences, ROI stories for economic buyers, and the calls that are hard to make alone.

What you can expect

Hands-on. I design and prototype myself, not just review

Decisions on paper. autonomy policies, principles and specs your team keeps after I leave

Measured. we agree the outcomes up front, from time-to-value to adoption

Built to hand over. every engagement ends with your team able to run it

Proof

Vivian and Vida: an AI leasing agent and its operator console

Founding AI design at Property Vista: a design function built from zero

Oaken Digital: zero-touch account opening from 20% to 83%

How I think about agents, design leadership and teams

How to start

Email me a few lines on what you’re building and where it’s stuck. We’ll start with a 30-minute call, and if there’s a fit I’ll send a short proposal with scope, timing and outcomes within a week.

# Vivian – Zero-touch lead to lease — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work/vivian-zero-touch-lease.html

Vivian – Zero-touch lead to lease — Varun Velhankar

← Projects
Property Vista · 2026 · AI agents · Proptech

Vivian – Zero-touch lead to lease

A renter goes from a first question on a property website to a signed lease inside one conversation with Vivian. No forms to fill in, no waiting on office hours. The leasing team only sees the files that need a person.

Role
Head of Design, Property Vista. Design direction, prototyping, research synthesis
Product
Vida, the AI leasing and resident platform for multifamily and student housing
Surfaces
Website chat widget, full-screen chat, phone web app, operator review queue
Status
Live. Version 1 is a single linear flow

60%Faster time-to-lease92%Of inquiries handled without staff2Enterprise deals supported by the ROI views
Results from properties running Vida
4.4xHigher lead-to-appointment conversion2xFaster time to tour95%After-hours calls answered live

 First touch. Vivian opens on the property's own availability page, says what she is and what she keeps, and offers three ways to start. Units without photos fall back to a labelled placeholder, so a data gap never breaks the page.

 Most leasing software is a set of forms in front of a set of queues. The renter fills in an application, staff re-key it into the next system, and every exception waits for someone to notice it. We ran discovery with operators, walking the application-to-lease process from both the staff side and the renter side.

 What staff told us

 Leases get assembled by hand. Parking concessions and addenda are attached one at a time, then signed documents are uploaded into the property management system manually.

 Every application looks the same in the queue until someone opens it, so the risky file and the clean one wait in the same line.

 Screening, signing and payment live in separate tools, and the handoffs between them are where files stall.

 What renters run into

 The same details, typed again and again across inquiry, application and lease.

 Fees that read alike. An application fee and a holding fee mean different things and are easy to confuse.

 Households that don't fit one form. Co-applicants, children and guarantors each need something different from the flow.

 Instead of a smarter form, Vivian runs the whole lease and the screens appear when the conversation needs them. Leasing and residency are one journey, so the same conversation keeps going after move-in.

 One conversation, many channels
Web chat, text and voice are views of the same conversation with Vivian, not three products.

 Collect as you go, confirm once
Vivian gathers what the application needs while answering questions, so the last step is a review and one tap.

 Rails, not a blank box
Reply buttons keep the flow moving. Typing in your own words always works too.

 Leave and come back
The conversation outlives the browser tab. Nothing is asked twice.

 Identity at the moment of commitment
Browsing needs nothing. Contact details and verification appear when a price is held or money moves.

 A person when it matters
Vivian handles the file first. Staff get it, with the full conversation, when judgement is needed or the renter asks.

 How it evolved

 Six iterations, from a checkout form to a lease inside the chat

 Each step is a working prototype, not a static mock. Pick one to see what we built, what it taught us and what changed next.

 Play overview30 seconds, no sound. The tabs below cover each iteration in detail.

 1Form-first checkout

2Chat qualifies, form closes

3The whole lease in one conversation

4One session, every view

5Approval isn't binary

6The operator's side

Form-first checkout
What we built
Apply, status, and sign and pay as a three-step checkout. Vivian sat in a side rail, checking income against the threshold and offering to autofill the form.
What it taught us
The renter still did the data entry. Vivian was helping with a task the product shouldn't have asked for in the first place.
What changed next
Move the front half of the job into the conversation.

Chat qualifies, form closes
What we built
Vivian ran inquiry, matching, tour or skip, pre-qualification and identity and income checks in chat, then handed over a prefilled application. On a phone that became a four-card page. Text and email links opened the same chat on a phone.
What it taught us
The handoff was the seam. Everything after it turned back into a form, and the renter switched from talking to filling in.
What changed next
Keep the renter in the conversation all the way to signature.

The whole lease in one conversation
What we built
Lease review, signing and payment moved into the chat, with a file panel beside it showing everything Vivian had collected. Then a first-touch version for a stranger arriving from the marketing site, with no name, no phone and no unit.
What it taught us
A stranger needs answers before a price, and a price before an ask. Five household shapes were more than a first-touch flow could carry.
What changed next
Vivian asks before she prices, collects contact details only when she first needs them, and the flow carries three household shapes instead of five.

One session, every view
What we built
Usability testing showed the widget and the full view were two different conversations: expanding replayed a stripped copy. We rebuilt it as one session that every view frames: the widget, expanded, a pop-out window, the standalone chat and the phone.
What it taught us
Continuity is the product. Any seam between views reads to the renter as starting over.
What changed next
Twelve numbered fixes, from expand-in-place by default to a resume link and a one-tap re-price when a quote lapses.

Approval isn't binary
What we built
Approved with a condition became a designed path: a co-signer or a third-party rent guarantee compared side by side, the home held during review, and a deposit alternative at move-in.
What it taught us
The riskiest moment for a zero-touch lease isn't the decline, it's the maybe. Without a path through it, every conditional approval turns into a phone call.
What changed next
Eight guarantee and deposit cases, each reachable in the prototype, including the guarantee declined and the renter who leaves mid-review.

The operator's side
What we built
Applications Vivian completes land in one review queue with the file beside the list. Escalations arrive with the conversation attached.
What it taught us
Staff trust a score only when they can see what's behind it, and a decline has legal weight, so it has to carry a reason.
What changed next
Per-property auto-approval thresholds and policy rules decide what Vivian completes on her own.

 Inside the current design

 The decisions that make zero-touch hold up

 One conversation, every view

 The widget is not a smaller copy of the chat. It is the chat, mounted once and reframed as the renter expands it, pops it out or opens it on a phone.

 Expanding in place is the default. Nothing is copied or replayed.

 The offer to expand appears once, on the first rich card, and says what you gain.

 Declining is answered once and remembered for the session.

 A blocked pop-up quietly falls back to expanding in place.

 Closing a pop-out window hands everything back to the widget, with a marker in the thread.

 On a phone, the full view is its own page, and leaving returns to the listings.

 In the widget: a direct answer, with the catch stated up front.

 Expanded: the same thread, with room for photos and the floor plan.

 Ask for identity only when it's needed

 No account, no password, no sign-up wall in front of the listings. The first time Vivian needs to reach the renter, to hold a price or send a quote, she says why and asks inside the thread. A one-time code confirms the contact. Coming back later rides the resume link, so the renter is never asked to log in to continue.

 The reason comes before the request: "To hold it and send you the quote, I need a way to reach you."

 The lease arrives in the conversation

 The lease is a message and a document at once: the PDF, a tab for each addendum, and signing progress. Every addendum traces back to something the renter said, such as a parking stall, a dog or the move-in special, and Vivian says so. Initials sit on the pages that create obligations, and each leaseholder signs on their own link.

 Three addenda, each because of an answer the renter gave earlier.

 Approval isn't a yes or a no

 Screening often comes back approved with a condition. Vivian states the condition in plain words and puts both ways through side by side: a co-signer the renter knows, or a third-party rent guarantee, each with fee, cover and timing. The home and the quote are held while the guarantee is reviewed. At move-in, a deposit alternative sits next to the deposit with what is due today. A decline comes with a plain reason, the formal notice, and a person.

 Approved on one condition, with two ways through.

 A decline that names the reason and offers a person.

 A person, without starting over

 Asking for a human is always one tap away. Vivian names who and when, and passes the conversation so the renter repeats nothing. On the operator side the escalation lands with the whole thread attached, not as a cold task.

 Handoff with a name, a reason and no repetition.

 Coming back days later

 Renters rarely finish in one sitting. The conversation is kept longer than the price lock, so a renter who returns after five days picks up where they left off. One who returns after the quote lapsed gets a one-tap re-price instead of starting again.

 Back after five days. Nothing re-asked.

 The quote lapsed, the conversation didn't.

 Every edge case has a switch

 If a case can't be reached in a demo, it doesn't get built. The prototype puts each one behind an edge-case menu, so product, engineering and QA test the same states we designed.

 Next step

 Applications Vivian completes land in one review queue, labelled with where they came from. The file opens beside the list, so a leasing manager never loses their place. Two rules hold everywhere: a score never appears without its breakdown, and a decline needs a written reason, because it sends a formal notice to the applicant. Auto-approval thresholds and policy rules are set per property, which decides what Vivian completes on her own and what comes to a person.

 Applications queue. The household, documents and score breakdown open next to the list, with approve, approve with conditions and decline at hand.

 Escalations. Each row says why Vivian handed it over, and the conversation comes with it.

 What zero-touch lease is judged on

 MeasureWhy it mattersDirection

 Leasing rules change from province to province and state to state. Version 1 ships one linear path, the same steps for every renter, so it stays predictable while we learn where operators need to bend it.

 Next comes a flow each operator shapes with their own policies, with rent-table items such as parking and pets priced inside the conversation instead of added by staff afterwards.

 What I'd tell the next team

 The widget isn't a preview of the product. It is the product.
Our first widget ran its own small conversation and replayed a copy when expanded. A usability pass caught it, and the rebuild made one session that every view frames.

 Ask at the moment of need, and say why.
Browsing stays open to anyone. The request for contact details lands when the renter has a reason to give them.

 If QA can't reach a case, it doesn't exist.
Putting every edge case behind a switch turned the prototype into the spec engineering builds from.

# Inspector App Redesign — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work/inspector-app-redesign.html

Inspector App Redesign — Varun Velhankar

← Projects
Property Vista · Vida · Case study

Inspector App Redesign

Varun, Head of Design · Nov 12, 2026

Contents
TL;DR
Context and problem
Previous state
Approach
Current state
Redesigned screens
Status system
Design system and foundational blocks
Workflow impact
Offline and weak signal
Metrics and KPIs
Assumptions, risks and next steps

TL;DR

The redesign turns the Inspector App from a form staff abandon for paper into one that finishes a move-in or move-out in one visit, with or without signal.

Find today's work: the default Open view cuts the list from 47 rows to 5 in the prototype's sample property (−89%), sorted by due date.

Fewer interactions: a full move-in drops from an est. 132 taps and scrolls to 94 on phone (−29%) and 86 on iPad (−35%).

Photos: documenting an item with 3 photos drops from an est. 11 taps to 5 (−55%) with burst capture.

Offline: every tap saves to the device first. Re-keying from paper, an est. 12–17 min per inspection on weak-signal sites, goes to zero.

Submission: the "Inspection already submitted" dead end is gone. Every blocker is named, grouped by room and one tap away.

Estimates come from a step-by-step model of the redesigned flows (see Workflow impact). Production KPIs, each baselined before release, are in Metrics and KPIs.

Context and problem

The app could not produce its core output: a completed, trusted inspection record. Staff fell back to paper on several active accounts.

Who uses it. Site staff, leasing agents and property managers run move-in, move-out, annual and building inspections. They walk units one-handed, often in townhomes, mobile homes and basements with no shared Wi-Fi.

What customers reported

Account
What broke
What staff did instead

Metcap
Every field mandatory, including move-out fields on a move-in. After fixing flagged items: "Ops! Inspection already submitted."
Could not submit. Paper.

Metcap
Move-out interest not calculated; manual interest missing from report totals
Paper deposit confirmation

FSR
A dropped connection wiped all progress mid-inspection
Paper checklists, separate photos, re-key later

FSR
Phone form too small to fill out
Bought iPads for leasing agents

SKPM ($768k ARR)
Today's move-ins buried in full inspection history; staff scroll the whole list
Support tickets from staff who assumed the app was frozen

The workaround for photos was "get full bars before you tap Submit." That is a field instruction, not a product.

Previous state

The legacy app showed everything, labelled little, and saved nothing until the server answered. Audit of the production screens (Aug 2026):

Inspection stuck; redone on paper

Inspections list
Inspection details
All Rooms
Select Comments

Approach

Five rules drove every screen decision:

Work comes to the inspector. The list opens on what is open, sorted by due date. History stays in History.

The device is the record until the server confirms. Every rating, comment, signature and photo saves locally on the tap.

Never block without a path. If something stops submit, the app names it, groups it by room and links to it.

Ask only what applies. Templates follow inspection type. Rating scales follow item type. N/A is on every mandatory item.

One status vocabulary. Six states, one pill, one header strip, used on the list, the inspection and Uploads.

How it was built. The team ran a solo, AI-assisted loop with no research team: screenshot audit and customer tickets, then a Jira epic with eight stories, then Claude Design prompts per surface. The output is a clickable prototype with a network switch (Offline, Weak, Online) that shows sync behaviour live. Field validation with Metcap and FSR is next.

Current state

Every legacy failure in the audit maps to a designed, clickable fix in the Inspector App prototype (open it).

Redesigned screens

Each redesigned screen answers one legacy failure. Renders come from the clickable prototype, set to Offline, which is the hardest case.

Finding work

The legacy list opened on the archive. The redesign opens on the worklist: Open by default, with a count on every scope chip so staff see the size of the day before they scroll. The offline banner names the last sync time, so a stale list never reads as a frozen app.

Before
After

Inspection progress

The legacy inspection opened on unlabelled fields and a waste-vendor dropdown. The redesign opens on rooms, each with a progress bar and an "N missing" flag. The strip under the header says what is saved and what is queued.

Before
After

Rating an item

Three scales in a row made staff tap by position. Now one control has three variants by item type. N/A sits apart in a dashed, neutral box. Mark Section N/A clears an absent room in one tap, and Poor or Missing asks for a photo.

Before
After

Submit, deposit and sync

These surfaces had no legacy equivalent; the work happened on paper or not at all. Submit opens a review sheet listing what is left by room, with Go on each row. The deposit is a ledger read from the tenant record. Uploads lists unsynced work worst first, logout names what would be lost, and a submitted inspection opens read-only.

Submit review
Deposit ledger
Sync centre
Logout warning

iPad

Rooms on the left, items on the right, comments as a third column. The comment sheet narrows the items pane instead of covering the item it annotates.

Status system

Six states replace one orange (!). The key move was separating lifecycle (where the record is) from urgency (whether the inspector is late).

Decisions

One lifecycle: Draft → Queued to submit → Syncing → Submitted. Retry moves Sync failed back to Syncing.

Overdue is a flag, not a state. It rides only on Draft, as a compound pill: "Overdue 3 days | Draft".

The due clock stops on the device. Finished on time but synced late carries no flag. Weak signal never makes anyone late.

Red means act now. Solid red is reserved for Sync failed, the only state with an action. Overdue uses tinted red.

Never colour alone. Every pill carries colour, icon and label: 32pt regular, 26pt compact for list rows.

The header strip reports save and sync only. Overdue lives in the subtitle, so the two never fight for one line. The whole strip is a 56pt tap target.

Type colours are reserved. Unit orange, maintenance purple and building navy never mean status.

Status pill
When Overdue combines
Header status strip
In a list row

What the review caught against the first pass (board 1a)

List pills had no icons.

"Overdue" appeared twice in one row, as a pill and as "Overdue 12 days".

Not Started and In Progress collapsed into Draft; progress moved to "4 of 11 rated".

A green Submit button in the header read as Submitted. It became a navy button.

Filter chips (34pt), type filter (32pt) and rating buttons (46pt) sat under 48pt. Flagged for the next pass.

Design system and foundational blocks

The Inspector App reuses Vida's foundational blocks instead of a mobile-only pattern set. Building it also exposed four gaps to fix in PV DS + Foundational blocks before handoff.

Design system pieces used

Colour: teal #0e9090 for focus, active tabs and links. Navy #0d2b4e for primary buttons and the offline banner. Status green #1a7e3e, amber #e08c00 and red #c62828 on 10–14% tints, matching PVBadge.

Type: Inter only. 13/500 pill labels, 11/500 uppercase eyebrows ("SURFACES"), Title Case buttons ("Submit Inspection", "Stay and Sync").

Shape: 14px cards, 6px controls, hairline borders, shadow-xs on cards, the teal focus ring.

New field density tier: PV DS was sized for desktop admin. The app adds 48pt minimum targets and 52pt primary buttons.

Navy, not teal, for primary buttons: white on teal measures 3.88:1, under the WCAG AA 4.5:1 minimum.

Gaps to close before handoff (each is a likely QA bug)

☐ Token hex values are hardcoded, not referenced (#0e9090 appears 29 times in the prototype, 216 in the fixes board). Swap to var(--pv-*) or dark mode and theme changes break.

☐ Maintenance purple has no DS token. Add one or reassign.

☐ Amber text: DS specifies #b87200; the app uses #8a5600 on tint for contrast. Pick one.

☐ Promote three components used on 3+ screens: status pill (PVBadge variant), header strip (PVAlert variant), rating control (new).

Workflow impact

A full move-in takes an est. 29% fewer taps and scrolls on phone and 35% fewer on iPad. The bigger time win is what disappears: paper, re-keying and blocked submits.

Design model, est. · full move-in, 41 items, phone · assumptions below

Room navigation (16) does not change on phone. On iPad the two-pane layout halves it, taking the total to 86.

Model assumptions (est.)

Full move-in template from the prototype: 41 items across 8 rooms.

6 items photographed at 2 photos each; 4 canned comments; one 3-item section marked N/A.

Legacy photo flow per shot: Take Photo, shutter, OS confirm; plus one tap in and one back.

Legacy find: target sits halfway down a 47-row list at about 5 rows per screen.

Interaction = one tap or one scroll gesture. Room navigation = 2 per room on phone, 1 on iPad two-pane.

Ratings barely move (41 to 39). Savings come from photos, irrelevant fields, finding work and submit.

Offline and weak signal

Once a property is downloaded, a full inspection runs with no signal. That removes an est. 12–17 min of re-keying per inspection on weak-signal sites.

None

Rules the design holds to

Download a property from Uploads while connected; it then works with no signal.

Submitting offline runs the completeness check on the device and marks the inspection Queued to submit.

The due clock stops when the inspector finishes on the device. Weak signal never makes anyone late.

Photos upload one at a time, oldest first. On weak signal a small preview goes first; full size follows on Wi-Fi.

A failed photo stays on the device and on its row until it uploads or the inspector deletes it.

Logout warns and names every unsynced inspection. Primary action: Stay and Sync.

v1 assumes one editor per inspection; concurrent edits are not merged.

Assumptions, risks and next steps

Every number marked est. comes from the design model, not field data. Treat them as targets until the field test reports.

Risks

Offline needs the template, unit and tenant data on the device first. If staff skip the download, the app has nothing to work from.

The "already submitted" defect may share a root cause with retried saves. Engineering needs one idempotent submit path.

Auto-calculated interest depends on where deposit data lives (PV CRM or an external PMS).

Prototype interest rates are samples; confirm against the RTB before any customer sees a figure.

Rating buttons, filter chips and the type filter still sit under 48pt in early boards.

Next steps

☐ Pull the started → submitted baseline per client

☐ Instrument opened → finished timestamps per inspection type

☐ Run the airplane-mode iPad field test at an FSR site

☐ Walk the prototype with Metcap staff; validate the template list for move-in

☐ Confirm what the legacy Uploads tab stores locally today

Estimates marked est. come from a design model, not field data.

# Founding AI design at Property Vista — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work/founding-design-property-vista.html

Founding AI design at Property Vista — Varun Velhankar

← Projects
Property Vista · 2026 · Org, practice and platform

Founding an AI-native product design function

I joined Property Vista as its first designer and founding AI designer. The mandate fit in four words: frictionless workflows, faster time to value. This is how I turned it into a practice, a system and a seat at the strategy table.

Role
Head of Design, founding AI designer
Partners
VP Product, Head of PMM, Head of Engineering
Products
Vivian and Vida, across every channel
Since
May 2026

60%Faster time-to-lease92%Of inquiries handled without staff2Enterprise deals supported by the ROI views

The mandate

Two north stars

Frictionless workflow. Every task a renter, resident or property team does should take fewer steps than it did yesterday, and none should need a manual.
Time to value. From signed contract to visible ROI, as short as possible. If a buyer can't see the value, it doesn't exist yet.

In practice that meant owning the whole surface, from a renter's first message to the economic buyer's ROI report:

AreaWhat I own
ExperienceEnd-to-end journeys across every channel, IA, discoverability and feature adoption
ValueEconomic-buyer journeys, ROI visualization, executive dashboards and reporting
CraftThe design system, engineering handoff, AI prototypes and motion demos for customers
SignalCustomer advisory board, synthetic and solo user testing, the AI-native design stack

The case I made

In my first weeks I wrote two short memos for leadership: how design should operate in an AI-first company, and how design and engineering should work together. Both started from the same observation: AI changes the cost structure of design. Prototyping is now cheaper than documentation.

The old modelThe model I set up
Linear phases and gated approvalsResearch, prototyping and testing run continuously
Artifacts as the way to alignTeams move by risk and uncertainty, not by phase
Process as a proxy for qualityLearning decides the next action

Process scales teams. Experienced judgment scales impact.

Operating model

Judgment over process

Start where uncertainty is highest. Point design at the riskiest unknown first, not the first screen in the flow.
Do the smallest thing that reduces risk. A prototype, a transcript review, a five-user test.
Let evidence pick the next step. Learning decides what comes next, not a template.
Skip steps that don't add learning. Consistency in thinking, not in sequence.

Engineering

Design as an accelerator, not a gate

If design adds friction for engineers, it is failing. I align early on constraints, ship in layers (the MVP is the core decision flow, not a stripped UI), and hand off specs with every state and edge case, tokens mapped to code, straight into Claude Code and Figma Dev Mode.

For AI features, trust is part of the spec: make the why visible (sources, confidence, recency), separate facts from inferences and predictions, and keep a human in the loop by default.

AI-native stack

A design pipeline built around AI

PhaseTools and practice
IdeationClaude for requirements and wireframes; Figma MCP as the bridge; v0 for component generation
DesignFigma, the design system, AI plugins, Claude for review
ValidationSynthetic user testing, solo sessions, accessibility audits
HandoffFigma Dev Mode and Claude Code, with feedback loops back into design

The stack (Claude, Claude Code, Codex, Figma Make) cut concept-to-prototype time from weeks to days. This portfolio was designed and built the same way.

Value and platform

Making value visible to the person who signs

AI products live or die on whether the buyer can see the return. I own the ROI story in the sales demo, the executive dashboards after launch, and the value-realization curve: connected on day 1, first AI-led tours and leases in week 1, ROI in view by month 1, and portfolio-wide expansion by quarter 1. These views were used in sales and funding conversations that supported 2 enterprise deals.

Can anyone find it?

As the platform grew from one agent to an ecosystem, I set Vida's information architecture around one rule: lead with what needs a human now, then everything else.

Vida sectionWhat it holds
Needs a humanEscalations, ranked by urgency and value
AgentsConfigure Vivian: tone, policies, autonomy
ConversationsEvery thread, every channel, searchable
LeasingPipeline from enquiry to signed lease
InsightsExecutive dashboards and reports

Signal

A design function without signal is just taste. Synthetic users give breadth: hundreds of simulated sessions across personas and edge cases in hours. Solo sessions with real operators and renters give depth. A customer advisory board shapes the roadmap, and prototypes and motion demos go back to customers before anything is built.

First 90 days

DaysFocus
0–30Listen and map: shadowed leasing teams, mapped every channel, made the case for judgment-led design
31–60Lay foundations: design system v1 with AI-state language, the AI-native stack, first executive dashboards
61–90Build the loops: advisory board, synthetic plus solo testing, prototypes in sales conversations

Outcome

A design function built from zero, with a seat at the strategy table
One design language for people and agents, including AI states
An AI-native stack from ideation to Claude Code handoff
Feedback loops from advisory boards to synthetic users

Mature design organizations measure impact, not artifacts.

# Oaken Digital — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work/oaken-digital.html

Oaken Digital — Varun Velhankar

← Projects
Fairstone Bank · 2023–25 · Digital banking

Oaken Digital: banking customers over 60 can finish on their own

I led the redesign of Oaken's digital banking platform, turning a costly, assisted model into a digital-first, zero-touch experience for a customer base where nearly 80% are over 60.

Role
Senior Manager, Product Design, leading a team of 5 designers
Scope
Onboarding, authenticated banking and originations
Platforms
Desktop web, iOS and Android
Company
Fairstone Bank (formerly Home Trust)

20% → 83%Zero-touch account openings, across channels68%Engagement across a 65K-user base80%+Positive user feedback, sustained 2022 to 2025

The problem

Built for confident users. Used by customers over 60.

The platform was optimized for digitally confident users, but nearly 80% of active customers were over 60. The result was confusion, high abandonment and very few straight-through account openings: only 20% were zero-touch.

Left alone, account opening would keep leaning on call centres and branches, older customers would lose trust in digital channels, and Oaken would never scale as a digital-first bank.

Research

What digital-first banks were getting right

Mobile-first, task-focused journeys with few decision points
Plain language, progressive disclosure and strong visual hierarchy
Success measured by completion rates, not feature depth

Competitors optimized for confidence, not intelligence. That was our gap.

Competitor landscape
Benchmarking steps, language and recovery

Discovery

Why customers were failing, not just where

Funnel tracking told us where people dropped off. To learn why, we went a level deeper: drop-off at every onboarding step, time on task, and form-level abandonment and error rates. Identity verification, document upload and long-form entry were the hardest moments.

The journey as it was, across the authenticated space

We spent a year building Power BI dashboards that joined API events, telemetry and app analytics into one trusted view. The app data was stark: 70% of applications started in the app were never finished, and only 3% of all applications were submitted there.

The core issue was clarity and flow, not a lack of intent.

Strategy

Four principles to design for zero assistance

Clarity over cleverness. Plain language and obvious next steps beat novel patterns.
One primary action per screen. Every screen asks for one decision, and only one.
Progressive disclosure. Complexity appears only when the user needs it.
Design for zero assistance. If someone would need to call us, the screen has failed.

The new journey: linear, explicit about what happens next, with progress cues

The work

Before and after

"When I log in, I want to immediately see what matters most, without figuring things out."

Before: legacy dashboard
After: one dominant action

Final UI: larger type, generous spacing, inline validation and reassurance at identity checks

The app

Underneath it all, an accessibility-first design system in Figma: scalable type, contrast-safe tokens, larger targets and reusable onboarding and origination components, mapped directly to code.

Validation

Usability testing with older users for comprehension and confidence
A/B tests on call-to-action language, layout density and step order
Engineers in discovery, annotated specs and sprint design reviews, so what we designed is what shipped

My role

I owned the end-to-end experience from strategy to outcomes, and led and mentored the UX team around one vision of clarity and accessibility. I partnered with Product, Engineering, Compliance, Legal, Analytics and Operations from day one, and used behavioural data and experiments to settle disagreements.

What I learned

Designing for the most vulnerable user makes the experience better for everyone.
Analytics tells you where; users tell you why.
Great banking UX is less about innovation and more about removing doubt.

Outcome

Zero-touch account openings rose from 20% to 83% across channels, with 68% engagement across a 65K-user base and 80%+ positive user feedback from 2022 to 2025. Digitizing retail enrolment cut paper-based enrolments by 50%, contact-centre call volumes fell, and the design system became the base for the next products, including the Deposit Broker Portal.

# Deposit Broker Portal — Varun Velhankar
https://www.varunvelhankar.com/work/deposit-broker-portal.html

Deposit Broker Portal — Varun Velhankar

← Projects
Fairstone Bank · 2025 · Enterprise B2B

Deposit Broker Portal: eight weeks of follow-ups to ten minutes

We lost a key investment client, and brokers told us why: slow, opaque follow-ups. I led the UX strategy and design of a net-new portal that made servicing transparent and self-serve.

Role
Senior Manager, Product Design: strategy, architecture and design leadership
Product
Broker portal for GIC and deposit products
Market
Canadian deposit brokerage
Scope
Release one · 170+ screens · SAP, DASH and Dynamics

8 wks → 10 minApplication creation and processing turnaround170+Screens in release one, on a new design system0Email chains needed to track an application

The problem

The product wasn't broken. The servicing was.

Oaken GICs and savings were competitive, and much of the money arrived through brokers. Servicing them ran on email, phone calls, spreadsheets and manual updates across SAP, DASH and Dynamics. Brokers could not see where an application stood, so they chased internal teams, and internal teams acted as human middleware.

That was a revenue risk, not a usability inconvenience: brokers move capital to whoever services faster and more transparently.

Servicing as it was: reactive, not orchestrated

Discovery

We mapped workflows end to end and interviewed brokers, servicing teams and operations. The same data was entered again and again, statuses conflicted between systems, and documents moved by hand.

Broker journey map

System flow across SAP, DASH and Dynamics

Strategy

Transparent, system-orchestrated, low-touch

A greenfield portal. 170+ screens on our new enterprise design system: a platform build, not a feature release.
Workflow orchestration. Status definitions, triggers, data ownership and exception handling aligned across SAP, DASH and Dynamics. Tribal knowledge became structured flows.
Principles. Transparency by default. Self-serve over follow-up. Automation before human escalation. Exception-based servicing.

"When there's a delay, I want to understand why immediately, so I don't need to chase internal teams."

The work

Confidence and control over decoration

Prominent lifecycle indicators and stage labels, critical updates first, timestamped confirmations and audit-friendly interactions.

Dashboard overview

Client profile, KYC overview
New application, funding details

Validation

Workflow validation with operations and edge-case scenario testing
Usability walkthroughs with broker representatives
Status states, triggers and error states documented for engineering, with components aligned to the design system

My role

I framed the problem as a trust and revenue risk, secured cross-functional buy-in, drove the enterprise workflow mapping and owned UX architecture across 170+ screens.

What I learned

In broker distribution, servicing experience directly affects revenue.
Transparency reduces operational burden.
UX leadership in financial services has to think in systems, not features.

Outcome

Application turnaround went from eight weeks to ten minutes. Brokers track every application without a single email chain, internal teams engage only on exceptions, and the gap that cost us a key client is closed.

Reverse Mortgage and Customer Journey Analytics — Varun Velhankar

Fairstone Bank · Two shorter stories

A new product, and a new view of the customer

Two projects told through the decks I presented them with: launching Home Trust's reverse mortgage, and rebuilding how Oaken understands its customers' journeys.

Role
Senior Manager, Product Design
Formats
Product strategy deck, data strategy deck
Company
Fairstone Bank (formerly Home Trust)

+42%Commitments secured, one week after the reverse mortgage launch1Shared source of customer data, in place of siloed tools

Deck 01 · Reverse Mortgage

From a compliant webpage to a trusted product

A crowded market and growing demand led Home Trust to introduce a reverse mortgage for Canadians 55+, launched as EquityAccess to build brand trust and fuel post-merger growth.

01 · Reverse Mortgage. Introducing the Home Trust reverse mortgage product.

02 · The opportunity. A crowded market and growing demand led Home Trust to introduce a reverse mortgage product that builds brand trust and fuels post-merger growth.

03 · Task vs. UX goals. From delivering a compliant webpage to designing a trusted, transparent experience that simplifies complexity and drives engagement.

04 · Competitive analysis. What competitors do well, and where they fall short, to find room to differentiate.

05 · An informed design process. A cross-functional, insight-driven process balancing business goals, brand integrity and user needs.

06 · The solution. A reverse mortgage product page designed for clarity, trust and accessibility on desktop and mobile.

07 · Early engagement signals. One week after launch: 7 pilot applications, 14 submissions, +42% commitments secured, +7% funding completed.

08 · Looking ahead. From early traction to meaningful impact, unlocking more adoption and funding.

Deck 02 · Customer Journey Analytics

One reliable view of the customer

Our data tracking needed a major overhaul: insights were fragmented, unreliable and hard to act on. A unified data source replaced the silos.

01 · Digital Customer Journey Analytics. Introducing Oaken Financial CJ Analytics.

02 · The problem. Our data tracking needed a major overhaul. Insights were fragmented, unreliable and hard to act on.

03 · A closer look. Multiple tools, siloed teams, no shared view of the truth.

04 · Why this matters. When the data foundation is weak, confidence, innovation and growth start to crumble.

05 · Data-driven UX. Great product design sits where data, empathy and gut feeling meet.

06 · We're on the right track. Even this early, we've seen what's possible when teams connect data, empathy and design intent.
